beginner: Beans grow best in rich, loose soil that drains well. The ideal is loam, a balanced soil that holds some moisture but never stays soggy. Beans need steady moisture while the pods are filling out, but wet, waterlogged ground can rot the roots.
seasoned: Fertile, well-drained loam. Beans set the heaviest pods in soil that holds moisture during pod fill yet never stays waterlogged, since soggy ground invites root rot.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Both sandy and clay-based soils work fine as long as they drain well. Sandy soil dries out faster, so you may need to feed a little more often. Heavier soil does better if you mix in compost or other organic matter, which keeps it from crusting over the seedlings as they push up.
seasoned: Sandy and clay loams both work if drainage is good. Sandy beds dry faster and may need a touch more frequent sidedressing; heavier soils benefit from worked-in organic matter to keep them from crusting over the emerging seedlings.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Stay away from heavy soil that drains poorly, and soil that forms a hard crust after it rains. A crust can trap young seedlings before they reach the surface, and water sitting around the roots can bring on the root rot that beans catch easily.
seasoned: Avoid heavy, poorly drained ground and soils that crust hard after rain. A crust can trap the seedling below the surface, and standing water around the roots brings on the root-rot diseases beans are prone to.

beginner: Beans like loose, fertile soil that drains well. If water sits on top of your bed for a long time after rain, work in some compost first to help it drain.
seasoned: Fertile, well-drained loam, ideally with compost worked in before planting. The critical trait is steady moisture without waterlogging through pod set and fill.

beginner: Beans do well in slightly acidic to neutral soil. If you have not tested your soil, a pH near 6.5 is a safe target and most garden beds are already close.
seasoned: A soil pH of 5.8 to 6.5 suits snap beans. A soil test is the reliable way to confirm both pH and fertility before the season starts.

beginner: Beans make a lot of their own food from the air, so they do not need much fertilizer. Mix a little balanced fertilizer into the bed before you plant, and feed once more right before the plants flower. Too much fertilizer gives you big leafy plants but fewer beans.
seasoned: Snap beans are moderate, light feeders. As legumes they fix much of their own nitrogen, so heavy nitrogen pushes leafy growth at the expense of pods. Without a soil test, work in a balanced starter before planting, then sidedress once just before the first bloom. Sandy beds or leaching rains can call for a second light sidedress.

beginner: A balanced vegetable fertilizer like 5-10-10 works well.
seasoned: Pre-plant 5-10-10 if no soil test is available; sidedress a nitrogen source before bloom.

beginner: About 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet of bed before planting.
seasoned: 5-10-10 at 3 pounds per 100 square feet before planting, per Clemson HGIC.

beginner: Beans get along with most vegetables. The classic trio is beans with corn and squash. The one pairing to avoid is planting beans right next to onions or garlic.
seasoned: As a nitrogen-fixing legume, beans leave the soil better for what follows and pair traditionally with corn and squash in the Three Sisters planting. The long-standing caution is to keep beans away from the alliums (onion, garlic), which are widely held to suppress them.

beginner: The traditional Three Sisters partner; corn gives a little structure and the planting has been grown together for generations.
seasoned: Corn is the classic bean partner in three-sisters planting. With pole beans the corn is a living trellis; with bush beans the relationship is looser, mostly foliage diversity and efficient use of the same bed. The benefit is structural and space-based rather than a measured pest effect, and since corn is a heavy feeder, the beans' nitrogen fixation helps balance the bed over the season.

beginner: The third Sister; its broad leaves shade the soil and keep weeds down around the beans.
seasoned: Squash rounds out the three-sisters trio. Its broad sprawling leaves shade the soil, hold moisture, and suppress weeds around the beans, while the varied foliage heights of the planting make it harder for pests to lock onto any one crop. This is a soil-and-space benefit; give the squash room so it does not swamp bush beans, which sit lower than pole beans would.

beginner: A common, easy neighbor that shares similar warm-season, full-sun needs.
seasoned: Cucumber and bush beans coexist comfortably: similar warm-season timing and water needs, complementary growth habits, and the beans' nitrogen fixation lightly benefits the cucumber as a moderate feeder. The added foliage diversity is a modest plus for pest disruption. This is a compatibility pairing rather than a strongly protective one, so expect easy cohabitation more than active pest control.

beginner: Onions and other alliums are traditionally kept away from beans, which are said to grow poorly near them.
seasoned: Onions and beans is one of the better-grounded 'bad' pairings. Alliums release antibacterial sulfur compounds that interfere with the Rhizobium bacteria living on bean roots, the very bacteria the bean depends on to fix nitrogen, so bean growth tends to stall near onions. Keep them in separate parts of the bed. A useful corollary: beans or peas grown before onions actually improve the soil for the following allium crop.

beginner: Like onions, garlic is a traditional bad neighbor for beans.
seasoned: Garlic acts on beans the same way onions do. As an allium it gives off antibacterial sulfur compounds that disrupt the nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium bacteria on bean roots, slowing the beans down. Treat garlic and bush beans as bed-mates to keep apart, and use the bean-then-allium rotation to your advantage instead.

beginner: Leaves that look skeletonized or lacy, with the tissue chewed away from underneath but the veins left behind. Both the spiny yellow young (larvae) and the round, coppery adult beetles feed on the undersides of the leaves, and when there are a lot of them they also chew stems and pods. The adult is yellow to copper colored with rows of small black spots on its back.
seasoned: Leaves taking on a skeletonized, lacy look as tissue is chewed away from the undersides, leaving the network of veins behind. Both the spiny yellow larvae and the dome-shaped, coppery adults feed on the leaf undersides, and when abundant they move on to stems and pods. The adult is yellow to coppery-brown with eight small black spots on each wing cover.

beginner: The Mexican bean beetle, a leaf-eating cousin of the ladybug. The adults come out of hiding near woods in spring, feed, then lay clusters of yellow eggs under the leaves, and several generations build up over the summer. It is worst in the Mid-Atlantic and southern Appalachian areas and is rarely a problem on the West Coast.
seasoned: The Mexican bean beetle (Epilachna varivestis), a leaf-eating member of the ladybeetle family. Adults emerge from overwintering near woodland edges, feed for a week or two, then lay clusters of yellow eggs on leaf undersides; there are about three generations a year, so populations build through the season. It is most damaging in the Mid-Atlantic and southern Appalachian regions and is largely absent from the Pacific Coast states.

beginner: Pick off and destroy the adults, the yellow egg clusters, and the spiny young, looking under the leaves. Done early, this works well in a home garden. Beans can lose a fair amount of leaf without losing beans, so you do not need to spray for light damage. If they get bad, an organic spray such as spinosad is labeled for bean beetles, and a tiny helper wasp is sold to control them.
seasoned: Handpick and destroy adults, the yellow egg clusters, and the spiny larvae, checking leaf undersides; this is effective in a home patch caught early. Beans tolerate real defoliation without yield loss (about 30 percent before bloom, 15 percent during bloom and pod fill), so light feeding needs no spray. Where pressure is heavy, an organic option such as spinosad or a pyrethrin is labeled for bean beetles; the parasitic wasp Pediobius foveolatus is sold for biological control.

beginner: Because most damage happens in July and August, fast-maturing beans planted very early or in late summer can mostly dodge it. The varieties Wade and Black Valentine hold up better. Clear and turn under the old plants right after harvest so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter, and move your beans to a new spot each year.
seasoned: Since most damage falls in July and August, quick-maturing varieties sown very early or in late summer can largely escape it. The varieties Wade and Black Valentine are tolerant. Work crop debris into the soil promptly after harvest to remove overwintering shelter, and rotate beans away from last year's bed.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft-bodied insects, usually green but sometimes black or pink, packed onto the growing tips and the undersides of leaves. Heavy feeding stunts young plants and slows them down, and a sticky residue may appear. Aphids can also spread virus diseases from plant to plant.
seasoned: Colonies of soft-bodied, pinhead-sized insects clustered on growing tips and leaf undersides, usually green but sometimes black, yellow, or pink. Heavy feeding stunts young plants and delays maturity as the insects withdraw large volumes of sap; a sticky honeydew and sooty mold may follow. Aphids also transmit the mosaic viruses of beans.

beginner: Several kinds of aphids, most common in cool, dry weather on small plants. They multiply fast and build up thick colonies before their natural enemies catch up. Warmer weather and helpful bugs like ladybugs usually knock them back.
seasoned: Several aphid species (Aphis and Macrosiphum), most prevalent in cool, dry weather on small plants. They reproduce rapidly, building dense colonies before natural enemies catch up; warm weather and predators such as ladybugs usually bring them down.

beginner: Blast the colonies off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap, which works on contact. Start as soon as you see them. Once it warms up, ladybugs and other helpful insects usually take care of the rest.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water, or treat with insecticidal soap, which gives good control on contact. Begin as soon as colonies are found. Once the weather warms, ladybugs and other natural enemies generally take over.

beginner: Lay down reflective mulch, which confuses aphids and cuts both their feeding and the viruses they spread, and pull nearby weeds that shelter them. Do not overfeed with fertilizer, since the soft new growth is exactly what aphids like.
seasoned: Lay reflective mulch, which disorients aphids and reduces both feeding and virus spread, and control nearby weeds that harbor them. Avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, which produces the soft, lush growth aphids favor.

beginner: Fine whitish or yellow speckling on the leaves at first, turning to a dried, bronzed look as they multiply. The clue is fine webbing on the undersides of the leaves. The mites themselves are tiny specks, easiest to see by tapping a leaf over white paper. They explode in hot, dry weather.
seasoned: A fine whitish or yellow stippling on the leaves at first, progressing to a bronzed, dried-out look as populations build; fine silken webbing over the leaf undersides is the giveaway. The mites are minute specks on the undersides, easiest to confirm by tapping a leaf over white paper. They build explosively in hot, dry weather, completing a generation in as few as eight days.

beginner: Two-spotted spider mites, tiny eight-legged relatives of spiders that pierce the leaf and suck out the contents. Hot, dry weather lets them build up fast, and dusty, dried-out plants are the most likely to be hit.
seasoned: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae), tiny eight-legged relatives of spiders that pierce leaf cells and suck the contents. Hot, dry conditions favor rapid buildup, and dusty, drought-stressed plants are most prone.

beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water to knock off the mites and webbing, and use insecticidal soap before they get too thick. Keeping the plants well watered and unstressed slows them down, and helpful bugs pitch in.
seasoned: Hose the undersides of leaves with a strong spray of water to dislodge mites and webbing, and treat with insecticidal soap before numbers climb too high. Keeping plants well watered and unstressed slows buildup, and ladybugs and other predators help.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist, because dried-out plants are much more likely to get mites, and keep dust down. Check the undersides of the leaves during hot, dry weather so you catch them early.
seasoned: Maintain even soil moisture, since drought-stressed plants are far more mite-prone, and avoid the dusty conditions mites thrive in. Watch the undersides of leaves closely through hot, dry spells so you catch the buildup early.

beginner: Large ragged holes chewed in the leaves, and on young plants, chewing around the stem near the soil that can kill seedlings. The adult is a small beetle, usually reddish or yellowish, with a few black spots running down each wing cover. The color varies a lot. Early-season damage is the worst because it thins out the plants.
seasoned: Large, irregular holes chewed in leaves, and on young plants, girdling of stems near the soil line that can thin the stand. The adult is small and variable in color, usually reddish or yellowish, marked with a handful of black spots set along each wing cover near where the two covers meet. Damage early in the season matters most because it reduces the stand.

beginner: The bean leaf beetle, which is rarely a serious problem in most home gardens. The adults chew leaves and stems, and young seedlings are the most at risk.
seasoned: The bean leaf beetle (Cerotoma trifurcata), rarely a serious pest in most home gardens. Adults feed on foliage and stems, with seedlings the most vulnerable stage.

beginner: Picking them off and the same steps you would use for Mexican bean beetle usually keep them in check. Beans can lose a good bit of leaf without losing beans, so light damage needs nothing. Focus on protecting young seedlings, which are the most at risk.
seasoned: Handpicking and the same measures used against Mexican bean beetle generally keep it in check; beans tolerate considerable leaf loss without yield penalty, so light feeding needs no action. Protect emerging seedlings, the vulnerable stage, where beetles are active.

beginner: Clear away the old plants after harvest and move your beans each year so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter. A lightweight row cover over young seedlings protects them through the risky early weeks if this beetle is a problem where you are.
seasoned: Clear crop debris after harvest and rotate beans to deny overwintering sites. A floating row cover over emerging seedlings protects the stand through the vulnerable early weeks where the beetle is a known problem.

beginner: Rust-colored bumps, mostly on the undersides of the leaves. Badly infected leaves turn yellow, wilt, and fall off. Stems and pods can get it too. It shows up in humid weather and can hit most kinds of beans.
seasoned: Rust-colored, raised spots that form mainly underneath the leaves; badly infected leaves yellow, wilt, and drop. Stems and pods can be infected too. It develops under humid conditions and can affect most types of beans.

beginner: A fungus that survives the winter in the soil, on old plant debris, and even on stakes used the year before. Humid weather is what lets it take hold and spread.
seasoned: The fungus Uromyces appendiculatus. It carries over from one season to the next in the soil and on leftover plant debris, and can persist on stakes or poles reused from a previous crop. Humid conditions drive infection and spread.

beginner: Pick off and throw away (do not compost) infected leaves and give the plants room to breathe. Where rust is bad, a sulfur dust or spray gives good control if you start as the plants begin to flower and repeat every week or two, following the label.
seasoned: Remove and destroy infected leaves and improve airflow. Where rust has been severe, a sulfur dust or spray gives good control when begun as the plants start to bloom and repeated on a 10-to-14-day schedule; follow the label.

beginner: Move your beans to a new spot if rust has been a problem, since the fungus carries over on old plants and stakes, and clean or replace stakes between years. Water at the base instead of overhead, give plants room, and pick a rust-resistant variety if it keeps coming back.
seasoned: Rotate beans where rust has been a problem, since the fungus carries over on debris and stakes; clean or replace stakes between seasons. Avoid overhead watering and space plants for airflow, and choose rust-resistant varieties where it recurs.

beginner: Black, sunken spots about half an inch across on the pods, the clearest sign, sometimes with a pinkish ooze in wet weather. The veins on the undersides of leaves turn black, and spots show up on stems too. It shows up in cool, wet spring and fall weather, not in hot, dry summers.
seasoned: Black, sunken lesions about half an inch across on pods, the most prominent sign, sometimes oozing salmon-colored spores in wet weather; the veins on lower leaf surfaces turn black, and lesions appear on stems and seedling leaves. It develops in cool, wet spring and fall weather, not in hot, dry summers.

beginner: A fungus that rides in on infected seed and survives up to two years on old plant debris in the soil. Splashing water spreads it, and cool, wet weather is when it strikes.
seasoned: The fungus Colletotrichum lindemuthianum, carried on infected seed and surviving up to two years on plant debris in the soil. Splashing water spreads it, and cool, wet conditions favor infection.

beginner: You cannot cure tissue that is already infected; pull and throw away (do not compost) affected plants and debris to slow it down. On snap beans, a copper fungicide can help if you start early, but keeping seed clean and rotating does most of the work.
seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy affected plants and debris to limit spread. On snap beans, a copper fungicide or chlorothalonil can suppress it when started early; cultural control is the mainstay for a home crop.

beginner: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Clear away all the old plants after harvest, and do not grow beans in that spot for two to three years. Water at the base and avoid splashing soil up onto the plants.
seasoned: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Remove all plant debris after harvest, and do not plant beans where the disease occurred for two to three years. Avoid overhead watering and splashing soil onto the plants.

beginner: Two related diseases. Halo blight makes pale greenish-yellow rings around brown spots on the leaves and shows up in cool weather. Common blight turns leaves brown so they drop fast, with no ring, and likes warm weather. Both hit stems, leaves, and pods, and both spread in rain and damp conditions.
seasoned: Two related diseases. Halo blight shows light greenish-yellow halos around brown leaf spots and appears in cool weather; common blight turns leaves brown so they drop quickly, with no halo, and favors warm weather. Both infect stems, leaves, and pods, and both are spread by rain and damp conditions.

beginner: Two kinds of bacteria, one causing common blight and one causing halo blight. Both start on infected seed, spread easily when it is wet, and survive up to two years on old plant debris in the soil.
seasoned: Two bacteria, Xanthomonas campestris pv. phaseoli (common blight) and Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola (halo blight). Both start on infected seed, spread readily in moisture, and survive up to two years on plant debris in the soil.

beginner: There is no cure once plants are infected; copper sprays every 10 days can slow it down. Water at the base, not overhead, and do not touch the plants when the leaves are wet, since that carries the bacteria from plant to plant.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; copper fungicides applied on a 10-day schedule can slow spread. Avoid overhead watering and do not handle plants when foliage is wet, which moves the bacteria from plant to plant.

beginner: Buy new, certified seed each year instead of saving your own, since the disease travels on seed. Do not grow beans in the same spot more than once every three years, and keep out of the patch when the leaves are wet.
seasoned: Buy new, certified seed each year rather than saving it, since the disease is seedborne. Do not plant beans in the same spot more often than every third year, and stay out of the planting when the foliage is wet.

beginner: Seeds that rot before they come up, or young seedlings that come up stunted, with a soft, watery rot at the soil line. The roots die and the leaves turn yellow. It is worst in cool, wet soil that makes the seeds sit too long before sprouting.
seasoned: Seeds that rot before emerging, or young seedlings that come up stunted, with a watery soft rot just above or below the soil line; roots die and leaves yellow. The damage shows up most in cool, wet soils that slow germination and keep seedlings vulnerable.

beginner: Several fungi that live in the soil and infect seeds and young seedlings. The usual culprits are Rhizoctonia, Pythium, and Fusarium. Cool, wet, poorly drained soil and damage to the roots at planting are what let them in.
seasoned: Several soilborne fungi that infect seeds and young seedlings. The ones usually responsible are Rhizoctonia, Pythium, and Fusarium species. Cool, wet, poorly drained soil and root injury at planting set the stage for them.

beginner: There is no saving seedlings that have rotted; replant once the soil is warmer and drains better. Pulling affected plants and improving drainage limits the loss. The main thing is prevention, since these fungi are already in the soil.
seasoned: There is no rescue for rotted seedlings; replant into warmer, better-drained conditions. Removing affected plants and improving drainage limits further loss. The real lever is prevention, since the fungi are already in the soil.

beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to about 69°F before planting, and use raised beds in well-drained ground instead of low, wet spots. Avoid damaging the roots when planting, move your beans around the garden each year, and clear away old plants after harvest.
seasoned: Wait until the soil has warmed to about 69°F at a 4-inch depth before sowing, and plant on raised beds in well-drained ground rather than low, wet spots. Avoid root injury at planting, rotate beans with other vegetables, and clear crop debris after harvest.

beginner: Small, soft, watery spots on stems, leaves, and pods that grow fast in cool, damp weather, join together, and choke off the stem. Affected pods collapse into a brown, watery mush, soon covered in white cottony mold. Crowded, overfed plants with poor airflow are the most at risk.
seasoned: Small, soft, watery spots on stems, leaves, and pods that enlarge fast under cool, moist conditions, run together, and choke off the stem. Affected pods collapse into a brown, watery mush, soon covered by a white cottony fungal growth. Dense, overfed plantings with poor airflow are most at risk.

beginner: A fungus that thrives in cool, damp weather and heavy, crowded growth. Too much fertilizer makes the lush, dense plants that trap the still, humid air the mold needs.
seasoned: The fungus Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, favored by cool, moist conditions and heavy, dense plant growth. Too much fertilizer drives the lush vine growth that creates the still, humid canopy the disease needs.

beginner: There is no home-garden spray for this one; you manage it by how you grow. Pull and throw away (do not compost) infected plants, and open up the spacing between plants and rows so the leaves dry out faster.
seasoned: There is no recommended chemical control for the home garden; management is cultural. Remove and destroy infected plants, and improve air circulation between plants and rows to dry the canopy.

beginner: Give plants and rows room for air to move instead of crowding them, and go easy on fertilizer, since too much makes the heavy growth the mold likes. Water at the base and avoid keeping the plants wet and packed together.
seasoned: Space plants and rows for good airflow rather than crowding, and go easy on fertilizer, since excess nitrogen feeds the heavy vine growth that favors the disease. Avoid overhead watering and the wet, still conditions the fungus needs.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while the plants are growing and setting pods. Once the pods start to dry and turn brown, stop watering and let the beans finish drying on the plant.
seasoned: Even, regular moisture from germination through pod fill, then a deliberate dry-down. Demand peaks at flowering and pod sizing; once the pods stop enlarging and begin to dry, ease off and let the crop mature dry on the plant.

beginner: Water deeply enough to wet the soil about 6 inches down. Deep, less frequent watering beats a daily light sprinkle.
seasoned: Enough to wet the root zone roughly 6 inches down; watering deeply and less often builds a deeper root system than frequent light sprinkles.

beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, and do it in the morning so the plants dry off during the day. Wet leaves overnight can spread disease.
seasoned: Water at the soil level in the morning so foliage dries before evening; this limits the foliar diseases beans are prone to.

beginner: If the soil is wet but the plants still wilt or the lower leaves turn yellow, you may be overwatering. Soggy soil rots the roots.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and stunted growth point to waterlogged roots and the onset of root rot.

beginner: If plants dry out while flowering, they drop their flowers and the beans come out small and tough. Keep the water steady at that stage.
seasoned: Drought stress during and after flowering aborts blossoms and produces small, stringy pods.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp, not soggy, until the seedlings come up. Bean seeds rot in cold, wet ground.
seasoned: Direct-sown into warm soil, bush beans want an evenly moist seedbed until emergence, but not soggy: bean seed rots in cold, waterlogged ground.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly watered as they get going.
seasoned: Grow the young plants on with steady, even moisture as they root out.

beginner: Water deeply to soak about 6 inches down, in the morning at the soil so the leaves dry during the day. Wet leaves overnight can spread disease.
seasoned: Keep soil moisture near field capacity, watering deeply to wet the root zone about 6 inches down, at soil level in the morning so foliage dries before evening.

beginner: Keep the water steady while the beans flower. Drought now drops the blossoms and you get fewer beans.
seasoned: Flowering is moisture-critical: stress here aborts blossoms and cuts the set. Keep the soil evenly moist and water at the base.

beginner: This is when the beans fill out, so keep the soil evenly moist. Letting it dry now means fewer and smaller beans.
seasoned: Pod fill sets the size of the crop. Keep the bed evenly moist here; drought while the seeds are plumping aborts pods and shrinks the beans.

beginner: Stop watering once the pods start to dry and turn brown. Extra water now just slows drying and can make the beans mold in the pod.
seasoned: Reduce water applications as the seeds begin to mature, then withhold entirely so the pods cure dry on the plant. Late watering only slows the dry-down and risks mold in the ripening pods.

beginner: Try not to spray the whole plant from above. The most important time to keep water steady is when pods are forming.
seasoned: Avoid overhead watering where practical; the critical moisture window is pod set through pod development.

beginner: The plants most need water while flowering and filling pods; a dry spell then means fewer, smaller beans. After that they need to dry out, so stop watering once the pods start browning.
seasoned: Flowering and pod fill are the moisture-critical stages; drought here aborts pods and shrinks the seed. The dry-down after pod fill is the opposite: withhold water so the pods cure on the plant.

beginner: You do not need to harden off beans. They are planted straight into the garden from seed.
seasoned: Not applicable. Bush beans are direct-sown in place and are not started indoors or hardened off.

beginner: Plant bean seeds right where they will grow, once the soil has warmed and frost is past. Beans do not like having their roots disturbed, so skip starting them indoors.
seasoned: Sow directly into warm soil after the last spring frost. Beans resent root disturbance and germinate quickly in place, so transplanting offers no advantage and risks setting plants back.

beginner: Use a good potting mix, not garden soil, which packs down too hard in pots.
seasoned: A well-draining potting mix; avoid native garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in containers.

beginner: Mix in a little compost for fertility.
seasoned: Blend in compost for baseline fertility; beans need little added nitrogen.

beginner: Pots dry out faster than garden beds, so check the soil daily in hot weather and water when the top inch is dry.
seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; monitor daily in heat and water when the top inch dries.

beginner: Container beans still need little feeding; a light dose before flowering is plenty.
seasoned: Feeding needs stay low in containers; a single light pre-bloom feed suffices.

beginner: Not applicable. Beans are a warm-season annual; they finish in one season and are not overwintered.
seasoned: Not applicable. As a frost-tender annual, bush beans complete their cycle in a single season and are not overwintered.

beginner: Bush beans grow well in a pot at least 5 gallons and 8 inches deep. Plant several seeds across the surface and keep the mix evenly moist.
seasoned: Bush beans are well-suited to containers given their compact, determinate habit. A pot of at least 5 gallons and 8 inches deep, planted with several seeds for a worthwhile pick, performs well with even moisture.

beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match for beans because it keeps the water steady, which is exactly what they like.
seasoned: A self-watering container suits beans well, smoothing out the steady moisture they want through pod fill.

beginner: A wide pot works better for bush beans than a deep, narrow one. Their roots stay near the surface, and the plants do best grown several together, so width matters more than depth. A broad pot lets you plant several seeds across the top so one container gives a worthwhile handful.
seasoned: A wide container suits bush beans better than a deep, narrow one. Their roots are shallow and run near the surface, and they crop best with several plants grown together, so surface area matters more than depth. A broad pot lets you space several seeds across the top for a worthwhile pick from one container.

beginner: Do not plant beans in the same spot two years running. Diseases build up in the soil and can hit the next bean crop.
seasoned: Avoid following beans with beans or other legumes in the same bed; rotate to break the soil-borne disease cycle beans are prone to.

beginner: Move your beans to a new spot each year, on about a three-year rotation. Because beans feed the soil with nitrogen, whatever you plant there next will benefit.
seasoned: Rotate beans on a roughly three-year cycle. Their nitrogen-fixing habit makes them a good predecessor for nitrogen-hungry crops.

beginner: This is how to store dry beans. When the beans are completely hard and dry, put them in a sealed jar and keep it in a cool, dark cupboard. They keep for a year or more. Be sure the beans are fully dry first, because even a little moisture makes them mold.
seasoned: The right way to store dry beans. Once the beans are storage-dry (hard enough to shatter, not dent, under a hammer), keep them airtight in a cool, dark, dry place. In an ordinary sealed jar they hold a year or more; with the oxygen removed (a #10 can or a Mylar bag with an oxygen absorber) they keep ten years or longer.

beginner: You do not need to refrigerate dry beans. Some gardeners freeze them for a few days first to kill tiny insects, then keep them sealed in the cupboard.
seasoned: Not needed once the beans are dry and sealed. A few days in the freezer before jarring is the usual trick for killing any bean weevils in the seed; refrigeration otherwise adds nothing.

beginner: Freezing the dry beans for a few days before you jar them kills any bugs in the seed. After that, store them sealed in the cupboard.
seasoned: A 3 to 4 day spell in the freezer before storage kills bean weevil eggs hidden in the seed; jar the beans airtight afterward. Sealed, fully dry beans also keep long-term frozen.

beginner: The most important thing is that the beans are completely dry before storing, or they will mold. A dry bean shatters instead of squashing when you bite it. Beans kept several years are still safe but get harder to cook, so try to use them within a year or two.
seasoned: The one rule that matters: the beans must be storage-dry before they go in the jar, or the batch molds. Test by biting or hammering a bean; it should shatter, not dent. Older beans stay safe but cook up harder and slower, so use within a couple of years for best texture.

beginner: The classic black bean and a longtime heirloom, a staple across the Americas for thousands of years (you may also see it sold as the turtle bean). Small, shiny, dark seeds with an earthy flavor. It is one of the slower dry beans to finish, so give it a long, warm season and do not rush the harvest.
seasoned: Small, dense black seed on a bush plant; an Americas heirloom that long predates modern cultivars. UC Davis lists Black Turtle at 105 or more days and classes it as late, so plan on a full season to dry down. Earthy flavor, holds its shape when cooked.

beginner: The everyday tan-and-brown speckled bean behind refried beans and chili. A dependable bush or half-runner type that dries down over a full warm season.
seasoned: Tan speckled seed on a bush or half-runner habit; a mid-season dry bean around 100 to 105 days in trials. The staple field bean: forgiving, productive, widely adapted.

beginner: A small white bean for soups and baked beans. One of the faster dry beans to finish, so it is a good pick if your season runs a little short.
seasoned: Small white seed; the fastest of the common dry types at roughly 85 days, at the early end of the maturity range UC Davis reports for white beans. Bush habit, a good choice where the season is shorter.

beginner: The large red kidney-shaped bean for chili and stews. It wants a full warm season to dry down.
seasoned: Large red kidney seed; a moderately late dry bean around 100 days, in the dark-red-kidney range UC Davis reports. Holds its shape well in long-cooked dishes.

beginner: A New England heirloom with striking white-and-maroon speckled seeds. It is one of the longest to finish, so give it a full season; good either dried or cooked fresh from the shell.
seasoned: White-and-maroon speckled heirloom seed; one of the latest of the set at about 107 days in trials (WSU). Dual-purpose, dry or fresh-shell; reliable in the Northeast.

beginner: Most dry beans are grown the same way; they just look different and take slightly different amounts of time. If your season is short, choose a faster type like navy rather than a long-season type like black turtle or kidney.
seasoned: Nearly all common dry beans are bush or half-runner forms of Phaseolus vulgaris, so they share this crop's culture; they differ mainly in seed color, size, and days to maturity. Match the variety to your season: navy dries down fastest, while black turtle and Jacob's cattle run the longest.

beginner: Bare soil for about a week, then a bent stem pushes up through the surface, pulling two thick first leaves (called seed leaves) up with it. Beans come up fast in warm soil but rot in cold, wet ground. If you plant before the soil has warmed to about 60°F, many seeds will not come up at all.
seasoned: Bare soil for roughly a week, then the seedling shoulders up through the surface still bent in a hook, dragging the two thick seed leaves (cotyledons) up with it before they unfold. Emergence is fast in warm soil but stalls or rots outright in cold, wet ground. Beans planted before the soil reaches about 60°F at a 4-inch depth germinate poorly, and a slow start invites seedcorn maggot and seed rot.

beginner: Wait to plant until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F. There is no reward for planting early with beans, only rotted seed. Plant about 1 inch deep in moist, well-drained soil, and do not keep the bed soggy.
seasoned: Sow only once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth; there is no advantage to planting early, and every advantage to waiting. Sow about 1 inch deep into a moist, well-drained bed and avoid soaking the soil, which suffocates the germinating seed and feeds root rot fungi.

beginner: Have your beans come up yet? Write down the date you first saw them break the soil.
seasoned: Have your beans emerged? Note the date to track days to maturity from a real sowing rather than the seed packet.

beginner: The two seed leaves open, then the real leaves appear, first a single pair, then the three-leaflet leaves that beans are known for. Once they are up and the weather is warm, they grow fast. This young stage is when beetles can do the most damage to the little plants.
seasoned: The cotyledons open and the first true leaves appear: a pair of single leaflets, followed by the bean's characteristic three-part (trifoliate) leaves. Growth is quick once the plant is up and the weather is warm. Young seedlings are the stage most vulnerable to bean leaf beetle feeding, which can thin a stand.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and pull weeds early, because small beans do not compete well with them. Weed and hoe shallowly, since bean roots are close to the surface. You do not need to thin bush beans, they are planted where they will grow.
seasoned: Keep the bed evenly moist and weed-free; young beans compete poorly with weeds. Cultivate shallowly, since bean roots run close to the surface and are easily damaged. There is no thinning to do: bush beans are sown at their final spacing and are not thinned.

beginner: How do your young bean plants look? Note any chewed leaves or bare patches in the row.
seasoned: How is your bean stand looking? Note any gaps or beetle damage on the young leaves.

beginner: The plant grows leafier and fills out to its full size, usually one to two feet tall, building up before it flowers. Beans make much of their own food (nitrogen) at this stage. You want healthy green growth, not huge dark leafy plants, which often mean too much fertilizer and fewer beans later.
seasoned: Steady leafy growth as the bush fills out to its full one-to-two-foot height and builds the canopy that will support flowering. The plant is fixing much of its own nitrogen now through root nodules, so vigorous but not lush, overfed growth is the goal. Overly dark, leafy plants with little branching signal excess nitrogen and forecast a poor pod set.

beginner: Keep the watering steady and do not add fertilizer now. Beans need very little, and extra fertilizer gives you big leafy plants but fewer beans. One light feeding right before they flower is all they need, and only in poor soil.
seasoned: Hold steady, even moisture and resist the urge to feed. Beans need little nitrogen, and adding more now pushes leafy growth at the expense of flowers and pods. A single light side-dressing before bloom is plenty, and only on poor or sandy soil.

beginner: How big are your bean plants getting? Note how tall and full they look.
seasoned: How are your bean plants filling in? Note their height and how bushy they look.

beginner: Small white, pink, or purple flowers open all over the plant. Bush beans flower in a short burst, so most of your crop is decided in a week or two. This is the most important time for water. If the plants dry out or the weather stays above about 90°F, the flowers drop without making beans. They start setting beans again once it cools off.
seasoned: Small white, pink, or purple flowers open across the bush. Bush beans flower over a concentrated window, so most of the crop is set here within a week or two. This is the moisture-critical stage: water stress now aborts blossoms, and sustained heat above about 90°F causes blossom drop, especially in varieties like Blue Lake 274. Pod set resumes once the weather cools.

beginner: Keep the water steady and generous while the plants are flowering, because dry soil now means fewer beans. Water the soil, not the leaves, to avoid spreading disease. If a heat wave hits, water deeply the day before, but mostly just wait it out, the plants will flower again when it cools.
seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through bloom; this is where water stress directly cuts yield. Avoid overhead watering, which spreads disease onto the now-dense canopy. In a heat wave, water deeply the day before and consider temporary afternoon shade, but mostly the plant will recover and reflower when temperatures ease.

beginner: Are your beans flowering yet? Note when the flowers opened and whether any dropped in hot weather.
seasoned: Are your beans flowering? Note the date bloom started and any blossom drop in heat.

beginner: Flat green pods appear where the flowers were, and the beans inside start to swell. Unlike green beans, you leave all the pods on the plant to keep growing. The plant needs steady water now, because dry spells at this stage mean fewer and smaller beans.
seasoned: Flat green pods set after the blossoms drop and swell as the seeds fill. For a dry crop you do the opposite of a snap grower: leave every pod on the plant. The pods lengthen, the seeds plump, and the walls stay green and pliable through this stage. Steady moisture now sets the size of the crop, since drought during pod fill aborts pods and shrinks seed.

beginner: Water evenly and do not pick anything yet. The pods you see now will dry on the plant later. Do not add extra fertilizer unless the leaves look pale, since beans make much of their own.
seasoned: Keep the bed evenly moist through pod fill and keep your hands off the pods, they are not the crop yet. Side-dress only if the foliage is pale; beans fix their own nitrogen, and too much feed now grows leaves at the expense of seed.

beginner: Are the pods full-sized with beans swelling inside? Make a note.
seasoned: Have the pods reached full length and started to fill? Note it to time the dry-down.

beginner: The plant starts to die back on purpose. Leaves turn yellow and fall, and the pods change from green to tan or brown and go papery. Shake a pod and the hard beans rattle inside. This is exactly what you want, so be patient and let the pods dry on the plant.
seasoned: The plant shifts from growing to drying. Leaves yellow and drop, and the pods fade from green to yellow, then to tan or brown, and turn leathery. The seeds harden inside and begin to rattle when you shake a pod. This is the point of the whole crop, so let it happen on the plant. Watering now only slows the dry-down and risks mold in the ripening pods.

beginner: Stop watering once the pods start drying, and do not pick anything. Keep an eye on the forecast, because a long rainy spell can ruin drying beans. If heavy rain is coming, get ready to harvest.
seasoned: Cut back or stop watering as the seeds mature to speed a clean dry-down. Do not pick. Watch the weather: a wet spell now can mold or sprout the beans in the pod, so plan to harvest ahead of a long rain.

beginner: Are most of the pods dry, brown, and rattling? Write it down, harvest is near.
seasoned: Are most pods brown and rattling? Note it, harvest is close.

beginner: Almost all the pods are dry, brown, and brittle, and the beans are hard. Now is the time to harvest. Pull up or cut the whole plant before the driest pods pop open and drop their beans, and before fall rains arrive.
seasoned: About 90 percent of the pods are dry, brown, and brittle, and the beans are too hard to dent with a fingernail. This is the harvest window: pull or cut the whole plant now, before the driest pods shatter and drop their seed or a fall rain sets in. Pods left too long split open and spill the crop on the ground.

beginner: On a dry day, pull up or cut off the plants once nearly all the pods are dry and brittle. If heavy rain is coming first, cut the plants early and finish drying them indoors.
seasoned: Pull or cut the plants at the soil line on a dry day once about 90 percent of pods are dry. If a hard rain threatens before then, harvest early and finish drying under cover, cutting the plants and moving them inside.

beginner: Have you harvested your bean plants? Write down the date.
seasoned: Did you harvest? Note the date and roughly how full the pods were.

beginner: After harvest the plants and pods need to finish drying, usually about a week. The beans are ready when one shatters instead of denting if you hit it. Beans that are even a little damp will mold in the jar, so do not rush this step.
seasoned: The pulled plants finish drying over about a week. The pods go fully brittle and the beans reach storage-dry: a bean should shatter, not dent, when you strike it. Only then are they safe to shell and store. Beans jarred even slightly moist will mold and spoil the batch.

beginner: Spread or hang the plants somewhere dry and airy for about a week, then shell the beans out by hand. Let the beans dry a few more days, then store them in a sealed jar in a cool, dark cupboard. In a jar they keep for a year or more.
seasoned: Lay the plants in a single layer or hang them somewhere dry and airy for 5 to 7 days, then shell by hand, or bag the pods and thresh by hitting the bag. Winnow the chaff on a breezy day, then let the shelled beans dry a few days more before storing airtight in a cool, dark place.

beginner: Are the beans fully hard and dry? Write down how much you got.
seasoned: Are the beans storage-dry (shatter, not dent)? Note your shelled yield.

beginner: Time to plant beans
seasoned: Time to sow beans

beginner: Plant bush beans right in the garden after the last spring frost, once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F. Plant about 1 inch deep in moist, well-drained soil. There is no benefit to planting earlier.
seasoned: Direct-sow bush beans after the last spring frost, once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth. Sow about 1 inch deep into a moist, well-drained bed; there is no advantage to planting earlier.

beginner: Plant your next row of beans
seasoned: Sow your next short row of beans

beginner: Bush beans give a big crop over two to three weeks, then slow down. Plant a new short row now, about two weeks after the last one, to keep beans coming. Stop planting about two months before your first fall frost.
seasoned: Bush beans crop over a concentrated two-to-three-week window, then taper. Sow a fresh short row now, about two weeks after your last sowing, to keep fresh beans coming. Stop about two months before your first fall frost.

beginner: Start checking your beans every day
seasoned: Start checking your beans daily

beginner: Most bush beans are ready around 50 to 60 days. Start checking every day and pick firm, crisp pods that snap cleanly, before the seeds bulge through. Pick every two or three days to keep more beans coming.
seasoned: Most bush beans are ready around 50 to 60 days. Begin checking daily and pick firm, crisp pods that snap cleanly, before the seeds bulge. Harvest every two to three days to keep the plants producing.

beginner: Frost is coming, cover or pick your beans
seasoned: Frost expected, protect or harvest beans

seasoned: Beans are frost-tender and a light frost will kill them. If frost is forecast, harvest any pickable pods and cover plants with row cover or sheets overnight. In fall, a hard frost ends the crop, so pick everything usable first.

seasoned: Sustained heat above about 90°F during bloom causes beans to drop blossoms instead of setting pods, especially varieties like Blue Lake 274. Keep moisture steady and water deeply ahead of the heat; the plant will resume setting pods once it cools.

beginner: Bean seeds rot in cold, wet soil. Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F before planting, because planting early just leads to rotted seed and missing plants. Beans planted into warm soil catch up fast, so there is nothing to gain by rushing.
seasoned: Bean seed rots in cold, wet ground. Wait until the soil is at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth before sowing, since early planting only invites poor stands, seed rot, and seedcorn maggot. There is no head start to be had: beans sown into warm soil quickly overtake those sown into cold soil.

beginner: Plant bean seeds right in the garden instead of starting them inside. Beans do not like having their roots disturbed and sprout quickly anyway, so there is no benefit to transplanting. Plant about 1 inch deep in moist, well-drained soil.
seasoned: Sow beans where they will grow rather than starting them indoors. Beans resent root disturbance and germinate fast in place, so transplanting offers no advantage and sets plants back. Sow about 1 inch deep into a moist, well-drained bed.

beginner: Pull weeds early, but weed shallowly. Young beans do not compete well with weeds, yet their roots are near the surface, so digging deep hurts the plant more than the weeds do. Pull by hand and hoe lightly near the row, especially in the first six weeks.
seasoned: Weed early and cultivate shallowly. Young beans compete poorly with weeds, but their roots run close to the surface, so deep hoeing does more harm than the weeds. Hand-pull and scuffle-hoe lightly near the row, especially in the first six weeks.

beginner: Do not add nitrogen fertilizer now. Beans make much of their own from the air through their roots, and extra fertilizer just gives you big leafy plants with fewer beans. At most, feed once lightly right before they flower, and only if your soil is poor.
seasoned: Hold off on nitrogen. As legumes, beans fix much of their own through root nodules, and extra nitrogen now drives leafy growth at the expense of flowers and pods. At most, a single light side-dressing just before bloom, and only on poor or sandy soil.

beginner: Keep the water steady and generous while the plants flower. Flowering and pod-forming are the times beans most need water, and letting them dry out now makes the flowers drop and the crop shrink. Water the soil in the morning, not the leaves, to keep disease down.
seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through bloom. Flowering and pod set are the moisture-critical stages, and water stress now aborts blossoms and directly cuts the crop. Water at the soil in the morning, not overhead, to keep the dense canopy dry and limit disease.

beginner: When it stays hotter than about 90°F, beans drop their flowers, especially varieties like Blue Lake 274. The plant gives up on flowers when it is too hot to make beans, then starts again once it cools. Water deeply before a heat wave, but mostly just wait, the plants will flower again.
seasoned: Expect blossom drop in sustained heat above about 90°F, especially in varieties like Blue Lake 274. The plant aborts flowers when it is too hot to set pods, then resumes once the weather cools. Water deeply ahead of a heat wave, but mostly let the plant recover and reflower.

beginner: Harvest all the plants at once when nearly all the pods are dry and brittle, before they pop open and drop their beans. Pull them up on a dry day, and finish drying indoors if rain is coming.
seasoned: Harvest the whole planting at once when about 90 percent of pods are dry and brittle, before the driest pods shatter and drop their seed. Pull or cut the plants on a dry day; finish drying under cover if rain threatens.

beginner: Do not pick any pods now. Unlike green beans, dry beans stay on the plant to dry out. Just keep the soil evenly moist so the beans fill out well.
seasoned: For a dry crop, resist picking. Every pod stays on the plant to mature and dry; steady moisture through pod fill sets the seed size, and drought here shrinks the crop.

beginner: Be patient and let the pods turn brown and dry on the plant until the beans rattle. Stop watering, and watch the forecast: harvest before a long rainy spell so the beans do not mold.
seasoned: Let the pods dry on the plant until they are brown and the beans rattle. Stop watering as the seeds mature, and plan to harvest ahead of any long rain, which can mold or sprout the beans in the pod.

beginner: Let the harvested plants dry about a week, then shell the beans. They are ready to store only when a bean shatters instead of squashing. Damp beans will mold in the jar, so make sure they are fully dry.
seasoned: Cure before you store. Dry the pulled plants about a week, then shell; the beans must shatter, not dent, before jarring. Beans stored even slightly moist will mold and spoil the batch.

beginner: One plant does not make much, so dry beans are grown in rows or blocks. A 10-foot row gives you about 2 to 2.5 pounds of dry beans to store. How much you get depends on the variety and the weather.
seasoned: Dry beans yield a modest amount of shelled seed, which is why they are grown in blocks or long rows. A 10-foot row of bush dry beans returns roughly 2 to 2.5 pounds of dry, shelled beans (USU gives about 20 to 25 pounds per 100 feet of row). Yield depends on variety, season length, and how fully the pods fill.

beginner: You harvest dry beans all at once when the plants have dried, not a little at a time like green beans.
seasoned: A single harvest: the whole planting dries down together and is gathered once, rather than picked repeatedly over weeks.

beginner: Bush beans are one of the most reliable crops for a first-year garden. They come up fast, need little fuss, and give a real harvest in about 50 to 60 days. Even a short row should give you a good pick, and the main thing that affects how much you get is keeping the water steady while they flower and form pods.
seasoned: Bush beans are among the most dependable first-year crops: they germinate quickly, ask little, and produce a real harvest in about 50 to 60 days. A first-year grower can reasonably expect a solid pick from even a short row, with steady moisture through flowering and pod fill being the main lever on yield.

beginner: Flowers fell off without making beans
seasoned: Flowers dropped without setting pods

beginner: The plant flowered, but the flowers fell off without making beans, because steady heat above about 90°F stops the flowers from being pollinated and the plant drops them. Some varieties, like Blue Lake 274, are hit harder. Letting the plants dry out while flowering does the same thing. It is a weather problem, not a disease, and the plant usually starts setting beans again once it cools off.
seasoned: The plant flowered but the blossoms dropped instead of setting pods, because sustained heat above about 90°F interferes with pollination and the plant aborts flowers it cannot fill. Some varieties, such as Blue Lake 274, are especially prone. Water stress during bloom has the same effect. It is a weather problem, not a disease, and the plant usually resumes setting pods once temperatures cool.

beginner: Plan your planting so the flowering time skips the hottest part of summer, either early enough to finish before peak heat or as a late-summer planting for a fall crop. Keep the water steady while they flower, water deeply before a heat wave, and pick more heat-tolerant varieties if your summers are very hot.
seasoned: Time plantings so bloom misses the hottest part of summer, sowing early enough to crop before peak heat or as a late-summer succession for a fall crop. Keep moisture steady and ample through flowering, water deeply ahead of a heat wave, and choose more heat-tolerant varieties where summers are reliably hot.

beginner: Seeds rotted or did not come up
seasoned: Seeds rotted or came up poorly

beginner: The seeds went into soil that was too cold and wet, so they sat there instead of sprouting and rotted, or came up thin and patchy. Bean seeds do not sprout well below about 60°F, and a slow, cold start lets soil fungi and a seed-eating maggot get to the seed while it waits.
seasoned: The seeds were sown into soil that was too cold and wet, so they sat without germinating and rotted, or came up as a thin, patchy stand. Bean seed does not germinate well below about 60°F, and a slow, cold start invites soilborne root rot fungi and seedcorn maggot, both of which attack the lingering seed.

beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F before planting, since there is no reward for planting beans early. Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds instead of low, wet spots, plant about 1 inch deep, and do not keep the bed soggy after planting.
seasoned: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F at a 4-inch depth before sowing; there is no benefit to planting early. Sow into well-drained ground or raised beds rather than low, wet spots, plant about 1 inch deep, and do not keep the bed soggy after sowing.

beginner: Big leafy plants but hardly any beans
seasoned: Big leafy plants but few beans

beginner: The plants grew big, dark, and leafy but made very few beans, because they got too much nitrogen. Beans make much of their own nitrogen from the air, so extra fertilizer just pushes leafy growth, delays flowering, and gives you fewer beans.
seasoned: The plants grew large and dark and leafy but set few pods, because they were given too much nitrogen. As legumes, beans fix much of their own nitrogen, and extra fertilizer over-stimulates leaf growth, delays flowering, and reduces pod set.

beginner: Skip the extra fertilizer. Mix in just a little balanced fertilizer or compost before planting, and at most one light feeding right before they flower, and only if your soil is poor. Let the beans make their own nitrogen.
seasoned: Skip the nitrogen feeding. Work in only a little balanced fertilizer or compost before planting, and at most one light side-dressing just before bloom, and only on poor or sandy soil. Let the plant's own nitrogen fixation carry the crop.

beginner: Beans came out small, tough, or stringy
seasoned: Pods small, tough, or stringy

beginner: The beans came out small, tough, or crooked, usually because the plants dried out while flowering and filling pods, which is the time they most need water, or because the pods were left on too long, until the swelling seeds made them woody. Both are easy to fix.
seasoned: The pods came out small, fibrous, or misshapen, usually from drought stress during and after flowering, which is the moisture-critical window, or from leaving pods on the plant past their tender stage, when the enlarging seeds make the pod woody. Both are easy to prevent.

beginner: Keep the water steady from the first flowers through pod-filling, and pick every two or three days while the pods are still firm and crisp, before you can see the seeds bulging. Picking often also keeps more beans coming.
seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample from first flower through pod fill, and pick every two to three days, harvesting pods while they are still firm, crisp, and before the seeds bulge. Frequent picking also keeps the plant producing.

beginner: You plant dry beans once and grow them the whole season, so there is no need to plant every couple of weeks like green beans. Sow after the last frost and give them plenty of time, because they need a long warm season to dry down before fall.
seasoned: Dry beans are a single full-season crop, not a succession crop. You sow once in late spring and grow the whole planting to a dry-down harvest in fall, so there is no staggered replanting. Give them the longest run of frost-free weather you have, since a late sowing may not finish drying before frost.

beginner: In colder areas you grow green beans in one long stretch. Wait until after your last spring frost, when the soil has warmed, then plant a new short row every couple of weeks. Stop planting around mid to late July so the last beans have time to ripen before the first fall frost. Frost kills bean plants, so the season ends when the cold arrives.
seasoned: Across the cold zones, bush beans run as one continuous season. Sow once the soil holds above 60°F and the last spring frost has passed, then sow a fresh short row every two weeks. Stop sowing in mid to late July, even where the calendar looks open longer: a late sowing meets cool, short fall days during pod fill and rarely finishes a full crop before the first fall frost kills the plants. The earliest sowings begin yielding in roughly 50 days, and harvest carries through until frost.

Spring sowings yield from spring into late May; the August sowing carries harvest into fall. The summer gap is not optional here, it is when nothing sets.

Sow into warm soil and keep moisture steady through the heat.

beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, plant dry beans Mar 1 - Mar 31. This is a one-shot crop: let the pods dry down on the plant through May 30 - Jul 9, then cut the plants and finish curing the beans before storing them. The Valley's drier summer is kinder to field-drying beans than the humid Gulf coast, though a spell of rain right at pod-turn can still spot or mold a crop, so bring beans indoors to finish curing if wet weather threatens.
seasoned: Dry beans in the RGV are a single spring planting with a dry-down harvest, not a fresh-pick crop: sow Mar 1 - Mar 31, per the RGV Homeowner Vegetable Guide's spring bean window. Pods begin turning and drying at about 90 days from sowing, with dry-down complete by about 100 days (May 30 - Jul 9); cut the plants as the pods turn and finish curing indoors before storage. The Valley's lower summer humidity than the Gulf coast favors field drying, though a wet spell at pod-turn is still a mold risk worth watching. Frost is essentially absent here, so the window is set by the spring planting date and the dry-down clock, not by a fall frost. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: TAMU AgriLife's Valley guidance is one Valley-wide calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

beginner: Dry beans are a marginal choice west of the Cascades. This crop needs a long stretch of warm, dry fall weather to dry the pods right on the plant, and the maritime Pacific Northwest's autumn usually turns cool and wet before that finishes. Sow toward the early part of the recommended window (May) rather than the later end, and when the pods begin to turn and dry, cut the whole plants and finish curing them somewhere dry and covered, like a garage or shed, rather than counting on the field to do the job. If you mainly want beans to eat, growing the same plant as a fresh snap bean is a much more reliable choice here.
seasoned: Dry beans are genuinely marginal in the maritime Pacific Northwest. The crop shares its establishment window with fresh snap beans (OSU Extension's Oregon planting-date table; there is no separate dry-bean listing, so this is a reasoned analogy from the same Phaseolus vulgaris entry), but its 90-to-100-day dry-down to full maturity needs sustained warm, dry weather that this region's cool, wet autumn does not reliably provide. This cell narrows the sowing window toward the earlier part of OSU's recommended range specifically for dry-down, rather than the full snap-bean window, to buy the crop the most fall margin available; even so, growers should plan to pull whole plants as pods begin to turn and finish curing them indoors, under cover, rather than relying on a complete field dry-down. There is no optimistic path here: this is a crop for gardeners willing to finish the job indoors, not a set-and-forget field harvest.

seasoned: Dry beans are grown as a single full-season planting in the Piedmont and Coastal Plain, sown once the soil is reliably warm in mid to late May so the roughly 95-day crop has a full, uninterrupted run to mature and dry down on the plant well before frost. Unlike fresh snap or pole beans, dry beans have no honest fall cycle here: a fall-sown planting would still be filling or drying when frost arrives, so the belt supports one spring crop only. beginner: Dry beans are grown just like green beans, but instead of picking the pods young you leave them on the plant to dry out completely. The beans inside get hard, and you harvest, shell, and store them to cook later. Common kinds include black beans like Black Turtle, plus pinto, navy, kidney, and heirlooms like Jacob's Cattle. They are easy to grow and keep for a long time once dried.
seasoned: Dry beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) are the same warm-season legume as snap beans, but grown on to full maturity for their dry, storable seed rather than picked young for tender pods. You sow once in late spring, let the whole planting flower, set pods, and dry down on the plant, then harvest once when the pods are brown and the beans rattle. Cured and shelled, the beans keep for months to years. Black Turtle, Pinto, Navy, Kidney, and heirlooms like Jacob's Cattle are all dry types of this one species, differing in seed size, color, and how long they take to dry down (roughly 85 to 110 days).

beginner: The beans are ready when almost all the pods are dry, brown, and brittle and the beans inside are hard and rattle. Pull up the whole plant on a dry day, before the pods pop open and drop their beans. Unlike green beans, you harvest the whole crop at once.
seasoned: Harvest when about 90 percent of the pods are dry, brown, and brittle and the beans are too hard to dent with a fingernail, ideally before the driest pods shatter or fall rain sets in. Pull or cut the whole plant on a dry day, then finish drying under cover if needed. This is a single harvest, not a repeated pick.
